issue_context.title: System.IO.Directory.Move claims to throw when the target already exists; however it does not do so reliably.
issue_context.body:
> Starting with .NET Core 3.0, the Move method throws an IOException in all platforms when the destDirName already exists. In .NET Core 2.2 and previous versions, the exception was only thrown on Windows, and other platforms could either fail or overwrite the destDirName. See C++ rename.

Unfortunately, the fix was made by inserting a call to `FileExists()`, which is broken. Even if `FileExists()` worked, this is subject to a TOCTOU bug. As a consequence, rename targets can be randomly overwritten.

This can be actually fixed in Linux by using the `renameat2()` system call; however I could find no solution for OSX.

This problem can also occur on Windows when talking to set-top NAS boxes. Two computers may be required to reproduce.
comments: cc: @carlossanlop @JeremyKuhne
Triage:  Any prototypes to improve this are welcome. We also can consider improvements for non-OSX platforms. Performance is a consideration, of course.
I can fix this for Linux immediately. I can't fix the Windows case for set-top NAS boxes. Better to just document the race condition?

> I can fix this for Linux immediately

@joshudson Presuming you can validate perf, please do :)

> Better to just document the race condition?

If it isn't solvable, sure.

Working on this, I found the following in File.Move():

            Interop.Sys.FileStatus sourceStat, destStat;
            if (Interop.Sys.LStat(sourceFullPath, out sourceStat) == 0 && // source file exists
               (Interop.Sys.LStat(destFullPath, out destStat) != 0 || // dest file does not exist
                    sourceStat.Ino == destStat.Ino) && // source and dest are the same file on that device

The only way this `if` statement can ever be true is if you have memory corruption, or the jitter gets smart enough to elide the zero-initialization of `destStat` since it's initialized by `out` (at which point if we still supported CAS I'd be filing a security bug, but we don't).

I'm taking this block out anyway because I need to push the test down to native code.

As it stands, the PR accomplishes the following:

1) The corresponding race condition for File.Move() is removed assuming at actually was a file and not a directory and hard links can be used.
2) File.Move() with an actual file is faster due to requiring two fewer managed->native transitions. The system call count required is the same.
3) Calling Directory.Move() is faster due to requiring one fewer managed->native transitions.
4) Calling Directory.Move() to change the case of a directory on a case sensitive file system now works again.
5) Directory.Move() no longer clobbers a file by the name of a target in the face of a transient network glitch (network-filesystem*).
6) The PR adds latent code to fix the race condition for both files and directories for almost all Linux local filesystems. The code is opportunistically activated whenever glibc version is high enough. It would be trivial to opportunistically activate at runtime if `#include <sys/syscall.h>` could be resolved from Kernel 3.15 or newer.
7) Any remaining race conditions are tightened as a consequence of having the check and the action in the same piece of native code. Also, splitting with a `SIGSTOP` is harder, but not impossible.

\* I have actually seen this fail in production, once. We lost data.
